idiom_name: ASP.NET Core policy requirement + AuthorizationHandler over ClaimsPrincipal
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the enforcement machinery: register a named policy with a custom IAuthorizationRequirement, implement an AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement> that decides against the current ClaimsPrincipal and the resource (the pending request), and apply it with [Authorize(Policy = ...)] or RequireAuthorization(); multiple requirements in one policy are evaluated on an AND basis. What replaces the classic role object is the requirement/handler pair: the separation predicate is requirement data - the initiator's stable subject id taken from the persisted request - evaluated against the approver's claim, and the handler calls context.Succeed(requirement) only when the two identifiers differ and the caller holds the release claim. The framework gives you the decision point and the principal; the workflow itself (pending state, expiry, revision binding) remains application design.
pitfalls: Checking a role alone ('is approver') without comparing the concrete principal lets a maker who also holds the approver role approve their own request.
Deriving the maker's identity from the request body or a header instead of the stored server-side record lets a caller claim a different initiator and satisfy the check.

Authorization handlers must fail closed: returning without Succeed denies, but an exception surfaces as a 500 rather than a clean 403, and a policy that is never applied to the endpoint protects nothing.
